{"self_assessment": "Impact: I proposed and drew the sketch the table built from: one line over the back to a flared tail and one round the belly, both leaving from the nose. That gave us a single connected run that could fall from one push. I laid the whole back line from the start domino to the nose, and then the belly's lower stretch out to the tail tip. Our check showed all 125 of 125 dominoes connected to the start, so the full fish should fall.

Execution: I checked the nose join once the back line arrived and confirmed the belly would get the fall. I split the long belly into two strokes so it could be built in parallel, and I added the second stroke to the sketch for that. I laid my stretch to pick up where Sofia stopped, and I inspected the middle after it was done. I then kept my hands off the table so nobody bumped anything before the push.

Collaboration: I kept the table's roles clear: Sofia on the belly, Omar and Jack watching for gaps and the tail end. When two people were about to lay the same stroke, I said so quickly so we didn't collide. I also explained that the push starts at the tail end, so the belly only gets the fall once the back line reaches the nose, and that helped Sofia time her start.

Leadership: I helped set direction early by getting a sketch on the pad that everyone could build from. I called the plan for splitting the belly and said where each person's section started and ended. In the last minutes I kept the table calm and hands-off until the push.

I believe my share of the table's result was about 40 percent, since I did the sketch, the back line and the lower belly, and the other three built the upper belly, checked joins and kept the table steady.", "my_share_percent": 40}

{"self_assessment": "Impact: My main contribution was quality assurance. I ran five close inspections of the build between 0:45 and 3:00, covering the back line, the nose join, and the doubled-up patch in the middle. Each time I checked how much of the table the push would knock over. I reported to the table that the whole run was connected and falling, so nobody spent time re-laying sound work. The final picture was a clear fish outline with the full run connected to the start, and my checks helped confirm that.

Execution: I checked the areas that carried the most risk, which were the joins where strokes met. When I looked at the doubled-up section in the middle, I confirmed it was connected and needed no patching. I then reported that clearly so the table could leave it alone. After that I kept my hands off the dominoes. With the run connected and the clock running down, I judged that extra handling risked bumps more than it would help.

Collaboration: I offered to lay the lower-tail stroke and, when Hana said she was already partway through it, I stepped back at once to avoid a collision. I then took on the check she asked for. I kept my messages short and clear, and I stayed out of other people's work areas so nothing got knocked.

Leadership: I didn't set the direction. I backed the fish idea early and kept the table focused on the goal of a connected run. I helped set the hands-off norm in the final minutes, which kept the finished fish intact until the push.", "my_share_percent": 12}

{"self_assessment": "Impact
I built the belly line (stroke 2), the lower half of the fish's outline. I laid it from the nose join in several steady batches, and it carried the fall the whole way to the low point of the belly. Before the push, the whole run of 125 dominoes traced as connected from the start. The belly is a large part of the outline the judge sees, so it matters for recognising the fish.

Execution
I began the belly as soon as the back line reached the nose, so the fall passed cleanly from one stroke to the next. I stopped at the agreed low point so Hana could carry on from there without overlap. After laying it, I inspected the area closely four times (around the middle join, the doubled patch and the back near the head). Each time I confirmed the run was connected and nothing needed patching. I also noticed the doubled bit on the back and checked it was still connected.

Collaboration
I proposed splitting the work so that no two people were on the same stroke, which kept hands from colliding. I stayed clear of Hana's tail stretch, and I asked Jack and Omar to cover specific checks. When the doubled bit came up, I asked about it directly and then recommended leaving it alone. Once the build was done I kept my hands off the table so nothing got bumped before the push.

Leadership
I took charge of how the belly work was split and made sure everyone knew who owned which stretch. I kept the table coordinated on the plan: build, verify, then hands off. In the last minutes I helped keep the team calm and focused on leaving the connected run undisturbed.", "my_share_percent": 30}

{"self_assessment": "Impact: I proposed the fish at the very start. It suited dominoes because its outline is mostly gentle curves and a judge can recognise it from the outline alone. That choice shaped how the table split the work: a back line, a belly line and a tail. The whole run was connected from the start domino, and the fish fell as one picture.

Execution: I inspected the chain closely at several points (0:45, 1:15, 2:00, 3:30 and 4:45) to confirm the run was connected and to look for gaps and weak joins. I also laid extra dominoes on the back line near the head, and they stayed connected to the run. Once the picture was built, I kept my hands off so nothing got bumped before the push.

Collaboration: I kept the table informed throughout, with regular updates on the state of the run, and I acknowledged teammates' work as it landed. When people asked me to stay off a stroke, such as the belly or the tail tip, I did so promptly to avoid collisions. I also flagged the hands-off rule early and kept repeating it through the final minutes, which kept the table steady and focused.

Leadership: I set the direction in the first seconds by naming the animal and suggesting how to divide the lines among people. I kept the energy up and encouraged the team all the way to the push. In the closing stretch I helped the table agree to stop adding to the picture and protect what was standing.", "my_share_percent": 22}
